utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Jadranko Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Registrar. Today is Monday, June the 23rd, 2008. I'd like to greet the witness who stayed over in The Hague during the weekend so that we can resume the hearing today. I thank him very much. I'd like to greet the accused, their Defence counsel, as well as all the OTP representatives and the people assisting us. We are starting with a 15-minute delay because the Gotovina Chamber was seized with a last-minute problem which took 15 minutes. That's the reason why we're starting with a 15-minute delay. I'd like to recall once again that when there are housekeeping or procedural matters those are better raised at the beginning of the hearing in order to avoid such problems. I know that Mr. Karnavas has a problem to raise, so I'd like to give the floor to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President and Your Honours and everyone in and around the courtroom. I don't want to make a big deal or a federal case, as we would say, out of this, however, we received some new documentation from the Prosecution that they wish to put to the witness for this afternoon. We received it as we came in to the courtroom. Now, I see no reason why this material could not have been provided to us earlier in the morning, either electronically, then physically for us to pick up, or physically and we have our staff over here working. They could have come and picked it up. But I do feel that I'm being sabotaged when I come into court and I receive a set of documents which I haven't had a chance to read because I did spend the time to read all the Prosecution's documents that they provided, all three binders. So I do read this stuff, and I would like to be as prepared as possible. So I would -- and I know that they're labouring under extreme conditions, as we are, but to the extent it would be possible in the future to avoid this or to at least let us know that documents are coming and if they have the electronic versions to provide those, I can glance through them. I just want to be prepared. And finally, we just received one more document, and it is not in English. I suspect they're not going to go through the entire document, but again if they're only going to use one or two pages of it, it would be nice for them to translate so folks like myself who don't read or speak B/C/S can fully appreciate the content of what is going to be put to the witness, and then I can do my follow-up research, if necessary, for redirect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. Mr. Scott, would you like to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Briefly, Your Honour. First of all, the material that was handed out was not as voluminous, although I grant Mr. Karnavas that probably this explanation wasn't given at the time it was handed out. We did find over the weekend a couple of the transcripts a couple of pages had been left out, and when we were going to supplement that the decision was made by the trial support team that rather than hand out loose -- several different pages some of them -- some of the transcripts were just copied again with the new page included. So in at least several of the instances it was simply a matter of including one or two missing pages, but the rest of the material remain the same. As to the document that's untranslated, Your Honour, we'd is simply -- it's a document that we have found and just simply have not had a chance to translate. I had hoped we might get some or all of the translation before court started this afternoon but unfortunately it still has not been possible. There are only small parts of the document that I have provided in advance to the translation -- in particular the Croatian B/C/S translation booth, so they can help us with the relevant portions of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Karnavas, after this witness we will be hearing Zarko Primorac. In the 65 ter list he's scheduled three hours, and then we were informed that you would need four hours. Obviously, if you need four hours with the following witness, we will not be able to finish with that -- with Mr. Primorac during the week, which means that Mr. Primorac will have to stay until next week. Do you really need four hours, or could that be reduced to three hours as originally scheduled? I know that there are 67 documents involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, we spent a lot of time over the weekend working with the gentleman. I don't want to commit myself, but I believe I can do him in three hours. My intention is to finish him by the end of this week. That is our intension, and so I was going to ask -- I know we started a little bit late today, but I was going to ask that if we would keep the procedural matters to a minimum, of course I'm the recidivist around here, we could finish the gentleman this week. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Mr. Scott, according to our calculations you have four hours and 16 minutes left. You have the floor now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon Mr. President and Your Honours and all those in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Akmadzic. I hope you had a reasonably pleasant stay in The Hague since we last saw each other.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was going through the documents you had given to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If the witness could be handed, please, Exhibit -- this is one of the loose exhibits that was just handed out a few minutes ago, in fact, 10509. And indeed, Mr. President, this is the one that has not yet been translated, but I think we -- I will be inviting the assistance of the booths on a couple of -- on several passages, and I again regret that we don't have the translation, but simply could not get them completed prior to court, because this was a document that we were looking for at the end of last week.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I put in front of you and you have the entire document, if you will, in the gazette version, which of course is in Croatian or what we call here Bosnian, Croatian, Serbian and these are the Rules of Procedure, as I understand it, the Rules of Procedure of the BiH Presidency as they existed or would have applied during the most relevant periods of this case or at least at the end of 1992, early 1993. And if you could just look at those just long enough. I'm going to ask -- I'm going to direct your attention to particular sections in a moment but if you could just look at that enough to just confirm what I've just said is correct, that these are the rules of procedure of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no reason to doubt it. I didn't look at the rules of is procedure from the Official Gazette. I looked at it as a document. It's difficult for me to identify it like this. However, as soon as you ask me a specific question I'm sure that I'll be able to pin it down and answer your question. I assume these are the rules of procedure that you're taking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. And for your assistance and the assistance of everyone in the courtroom I've asked to have attached to the back of the document, if you will, still in -- still in Croatian only or B/C/S only, but in large portions of the relevant sections so that perhaps it's easier for everyone to read, and I will be asking the assistance of the translation booth on these particular items. So with that in mind, sir, if I can ask you to look -- and you can whichever you like, you can look in the gazette version or if you turn to the back you will find the enlarged excerpts. If you would first of all go to Article 8. Do you have that, please?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, I've been told that this has been provided to the B/C/S booth. Could we have an English translation of Article 8, please? If anyone is listening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Wouldn't it be simpler if the witness were asked to read the article.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We can do that too Your Honour [overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think that's normal way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In my experience we've done it both ways, but I'm happy to do it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness, if you could read, please, Article 8, so we could get a translation of that.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I read it there's one thing I'd like to say. Regardless of the fact that we've identified these rules, the real rules, the proper rules of the socialist Presidency of the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was drafted on the 20th or 23rd of December 1990, regardless of the fact that I was there at the time, I don't remember us ever making any amendments to the rules of procedure, and I'm about to read out the article that you've asked me to read. "The provisions of these rules of procedure shall apply in everything" --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This is particularly being translated, so if you could be a bit slower, please.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The provisions of these rules of procedure shall be applied in of all aspects to the work of the Presidency in the eventuality of a state of war or in an imminent threat of war."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I ask you to next go to Article 10, and can you read Article 10 for us, please.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The heading reads: "The exercising of the rights and duties of members of the Presidency. Members of the Presidency have a right and a duty to attend the meetings of the Presidency and the meetings of the working bodies of the Presidency of which they are members and to participate in their work and in the decision-making process." Paragraph 2: "In the eventuality that a member of the Presidency is unable to attend a meeting or for some reason must, during the course of a meeting leave the meeting. It is -- it is his responsibility to inform about this in good time the president or the general secretary of the Presidency." Paragraph 3: "In the exercise of their functions, members of the Presidency may participate in the working body of the Presidency of which they're not members, however, without the right to participate in the making of decisions." Next page, paragraph 4: "If a member of the Presidency is absent from a meeting, it is his responsibility to familiarise himself with the matters discussed and voted on and must inform the president of the Presidency of his own position on the matters." That's Article 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And if I could ask you next, please, to go to Article 14. Would you likewise read that for us, please.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 14: "The member of the Presidency who participates in the work of certain bodies on behalf of the Presidency, or participates in the work of certain organisations and communities, has a responsibility to act in keeping with the powers, positions, and directives of the Presidency, as well as to inform the Presidency of the most important decisions and positions taken by those bodies, organisations, or communities." Paragraph 2: "Whenever necessary, a member of the Presidency may make a proposal for the Presidency to take a position on a certain matter discussed by such bodies, organisations, or communities in whose work he will be involved." That was Article 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. As to the first clause of Article 14, if you will, can we properly understand the import of that particular rule, sir, to be that for example if someone is a member of a political party or political organisation and also a member of the Presidency, the first duty or first responsibility of that person is to carry out his or her responsibilities as a member of the Presidency; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A member of the Presidency may attend meetings of the working bodies -- or, rather, state bodies or organisations. As for the discussion that takes place at these meetings of these bodies and organisations, as for any positions taken, this member of the of Presidency must then inform the president or the Presidency. There is a reference here to the president as well, but it's the same thing in this case, the president or the Presidency. He must inform his own original institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's an answer to a part of my question, but there's a specific earlier part. As I -- as I read the first clause and it may -- we may be about to lose it from the screen, but as I read the first clause does it not say that the person if he's involved -- involved -- excuse me. If that person is involved with other organisations and communities, his or her first responsibility is to act, and I'm quoting now at least as translated, "to act in keeping with the powers, positions, and directives of the Presidency"? Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as long as he has been authorised by the Presidency and whenever acting on behalf of the Presidency, which is something that the Article makes perfectly clear. Not on his own behalf but, rather, on behalf of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the second part as you read to us a moment ago was that not only to act first and foremost in his responsibility to the Presidency but also inform the Presidency of these other activities; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The member of the Presidency may make a proposal for the Presidency to take a position. That's how it's expressed here. "May make a proposal," which is not a commitment or a responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. If I can ask you then to go to Article 19, which is the topic that we have discussed extensively, and I think it's appropriate that the Chamber have this language in front of it. And is the import of this particular language, I'll ask you to look at it, is this the provision that provides that the president of the Presidency is elected for a term of one year and may serve two consecutive -- or two terms consecutively?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you agree, I might as well go on and read paragraph 1 of Article 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The president of the Presidency is elected by the Presidency from among its members for a one-year term. The president may again be re-elected for another consecutive term of office." Paragraph 2: "As to the modality of electing the president of the Presidency, this is something that is decided by the Presidency by a majority vote of its members." May I explain right away?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, sir, briefly, please, because time is, as you know, precious. Please go ahead but please be precise.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all let me say that the president is elected by the Presidency. This is unambiguous. The next thing I wish to say is this: Will this be a public vote or a secret vote? It's not specified here but that is the intention. This is something that is for the Presidency to decide. And the third thing, I believe the most important thing here, is that any president is elected for a one-year term and may only ever be elected for another consecutive term which means for another year.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And you just mentioned a moment ago, too, that this was -- the election was done -- or the decision was made by majority vote; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And as we discussed last week, if you recall, sir, your testimony was, and can you confirm again, that that was true for decision-making by the Presidency in general, that it was by majority vote?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in terms of these rules themselves, as you've explained last week and again today, so the term of the Presidency, the one-year term and the fact that the person -- the person can serve two terms as president, that is not a function or creature, if you will, of the constitutional law of Bosnia-Herzegovina but a matter of the procedural rules of the president -- Presidency; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rules of procedure of the Presidency do not run counter to the constitution. If that were the case, such rules could never have been adopted to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And based on what we said a few moments ago, that decisions by the Presidency were made by majority vote, can the Judges understand, then, that these procedural rules could also be changed or amended by majority vote of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what exactly the last article says. It might be that the very last part Article of these rules of procedure give -- give --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you were in one capacity or another. So isn't correct, sir, that the presidency had the ability to change these rules by a majority vote?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, I would like you to look next, please, at P 1 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Scott. We have heard several times the term "majority," and at least where I come from but I think generally one distinguishes two kinds of majority, a relative or a simple majority and an absolute majority. The absolute majority means that the majority of all the members of a body must cast their vote into one direction for the decision to be taken. The normal majority means that those who are present when the vote is taken are counted and more than half of those must vote in favour. Could you tell the Chamber whether when you speak of majority it is an absolute or a relative majority that is to be thought of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the rules, and it's been about 15 years since I last had a look, therefore it's very difficult for me to remember specifically, when we say a majority in the Presidency it means 4. That's one thing. The other thing is this: We have three peoples in our country and one must never forget that there were three peoples represented in the Presidency. There was a principle of harmonisation or coordination of votes, which meant that if a people, for example, opposed something regardless of the fact that the other two were in favour, then there would be a process of decision coordinating or harmonisation. That was certainly a step that was taken whenever a situation like that occur. This is a -- a practical thing. I don't think it's reflected in the rules but we knew all about our mutual relationships were of a highly sensitive nature. Whenever you have a community with several different ethnic groups, this is more or less a normal course of action to take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I thank you for the answer, but I must confess that I have not understood what you refer to when speaking about this harmonisation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This means that there would then be special talks about this in order to see why the disagreement occurred in the first place, and then this would pave the way, so to speak, for a final majority decision to be reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm told that perhaps if the gentleman could read Articles 45 and 46 it maybe of some assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Would you be so kind and follow this advice. I do not see anything -- any reason to object to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 5 says: "Different ways to reach decisions." Article 45 reads: "The Presidency takes decisions based on coordinated or agreed positions voiced by its members. Coordinating positions is the basic principle on which the Presidency takes any decisions." Paragraph 2: "Whenever there is a matter on which there is no consensus, the Presidency shall decide the matter by a vote. Decisions are taken by a majority vote of all the members of the Presidency." Paragraph 3: "When considering matters in relation to the equal rights of the various peoples and ethnic groups which will be enshrined in the new constitution of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Presidency makes decisions by consensus." That was Article 45. Should I go ahead with Article 46 immediately?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Article 46: "The Presidency makes decisions by a minimum of five votes of the members of the Presidency along the following lines: "1. Confirms a proposal to make amendments to the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. "2. Passes laws by decree. "3. Considers matters on the implementation of agreed policies in the areas of All People's Defence, state security, social self-protection, and international cooperation. Further, it makes proposals to the Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina on necessary measures for the implementation of those policies. "4. Establishes a plan of the republic's defence, and in relation to that provides appropriate guidelines in keeping with the law. "5. In keeping with the positions and proposals of the Assembly of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, considers any matters to do with the involvement of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the establishing and implementation of the foreign policies of the Socialist Federative -- Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the cooperation of the republic with other republics in terms of international cooperation within the framework of such foreign policies of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as have been agreed, as well as international agreements. "6. It reviews matters to do with cooperation with the Presidency of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, and with the presence or presidencies of other republics. "7. Based on previous consultations with the republic it proposes or nominates candidates for the president of the SRBiH government and for heads of diplomatic missions, as well as Judges of the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia from the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, confirms nomination for president and Judges of the constitution court of the B and H, and provides opinions on proposed appointments or proposed dismissals of the commander of the republic's Territorial Defence." That was Article 45 as well as Article 46.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Excuse me, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Not at all, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if we could next go to Exhibit P 10496.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It maybe one of the loose -- I'm told it's one of the loose exhibits, Your Honour. 10496. If the usher could assist, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you have that, sir, please, if you can just confirm that this is a record of a meeting of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 21st of December, 1992. It appears to be recorded as the 178th session or meeting of the Presidency. Do you see that? What did I say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Eight.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Then I have the wrong one then. 10496. Maybe the numbers have been reversed. It's different from the numbers I was given. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that exhibit appears to refer to meetings held on the 22nd of December, unless I've got it wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. The numbers have been reversed to the numbers that I was given. My apologies to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask you then to look please at P 10467.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: 10467. And I apologise, sir. That was our confusion. But can you confirm that that is a meeting of the 178th meeting of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 21st of December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And among other things we're not going to have time to go through all of this document by any means, but if I can just ask you about a couple of things. Throughout this document and indeed some of the other records around this time, is it fair to say, sir, that there was a continuing concern expressed both by Mr. Izetbegovic, by you, and by others with the repeat non-presence, the repeat non-participation of various members of the Presidency and the government?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that. On the basis reading this document, I cannot say anything, but I think that that's the way it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, for example, on the first page, at least of the English version, but on the first intervention by Mr. Pejanovic, about halfway through that paragraph or indeed the second sentence, for example, he makes reference to the fact that there are people who haven't been -- who haven't attended for up to four months. You see that as one example?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. However, some people were absent on the basis of a decision of the Presidency made at some previous session, and they were not told when they should come back. I think that on the basis of what is written here the Presidency did indeed discuss that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And continuing on into the document, and I'll try to assist you by referring to the person speaking, on the third page of the English version, but I believe the first instance of Mr. Ganic intervening,

utterances.speaker: MR. GANIC SAYS
utterances.text: "Let's say a minister has been absent three or four months. Nobody at the ministry can do a thing because of the minister's absence." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that the absence of officials was not only a problem for the Presidency but also for the government?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a problem, and it pertained primarily to the Serbs. However, as regards this statement of Mr. Ganic's, it did not refer to the government that I was in, because we know that my government was established practically at that time, and the minister could not be absent for three or four months when I talked to every one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Down below Mr. Ganic's intervention we have an intervention by you, and you say: "I propose four ethnic Croatian candidates, the ones to be provided by the HDZ." Do you recall who those four candidates were? Other than apparently Mr. Primorac, who's named. Do you know who the other three were?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this moment I cannot remember, but Primorac at that time had not been a candidate to be a member of the government. Primorac was not a member of the HDZ, and that's why I put him there. In the previous government and in this government not all Croats were members of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know for instance that Martin Raguz was not a member of the HDZ. He was a liberal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, there will come times day I'll just have to tell you, and without meaning to be discourteous to you, I will have to cut you off because my time is very limited and we have to move very quickly, so please bear with me.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, do you remember, sir, and we'll come -- it's actually mentioned later in the minutes, but do you recall that one of the four individuals that you were nominating at that time was Bozo Rajic?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. He was minister of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And he was a member -- unlike Mr. -- for example, unlike Mr. Primorac, for example, he was a member of the HDZ; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was proposed by the HDZ, but I don't know whether he was a member of the HDZ. I assume he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. That was actually my next question. In terms of the candidates that were being put forward, who were put forward by the HDZ, as you said just now, do you know what process the HDZ followed to put forward its slate, if you will, of candidates for these positions? And perhaps let me just go on and ask you as part two of that question, it may be an integral part of your answer, and then secondly, how was that decision of the party communicated to you? How did you know to put forward those four names?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The principle was that first of all I was prime minister designate. In order to form a government I had to carry out broad-based consultations. First of all, I conducted these consultations with the three winning parties. In this specific case the SDS had left the government, but some of its members stayed on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. My specific question to you, sir, please, again please be very direct in your answer if you can assist me, if you will, specifically the HDZ candidates, how were those persons selected, to your knowledge, and how was that information communicated to you? I'm not asking about the Serbs. I'm not asking about anybody else. I'm talking about specifically the four people whose names you put forward on behalf of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HDZ made these proposals to me since there weren't any possibilities for having broad contacts. The war was already there and the proposals I received were oral proposals over the telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, if you'll go down into -- further into the document where you will find another intervention by the President, and all I can say to the courtroom is that it's on page 8 of the English -- excuse me, page 5 of the English version, but if you can go down, sir, where you can find intervention by the President where he mentions the name of Delimustafic, and I probably mispronounced that, and Mr. Abdic. If you can find that statement, sir. And while you're looking for it and to give you time, the president appears to say: "If that's how it is, then there are four men here who are not coming to work. There are also the two from the Muslim ranks who haven't come to work since August. They don't even answer back, and they have nothing to do with the government. They don't even call." And then we have Mr. Delimustafic and Abdic. "This should change in the case of criteria and the people who don't come to work. Not like, I mean, ethnic structure stays the same." Then you respond: "There are others also who are not coming to work." But you had mentioned a few moments ago that it was primarily the Serbs, but you see in fact that Mr. Izetbegovic himself mentions two Muslims members that were not participating in the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One of the reasons why Mr. Delimustafic did not join the government that I had formed was that reason. Mr. Abdic was a member of the Presidency, so he could not be refused or reconfirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, finally I think for this purpose if you can go to -- in the English version it would be on page 6. If you can find another intervention by the president, sir, where he says: "I would leave the deputy arrangement for tomorrow or the day after. Let's stay with the four ministers. Let's have some criteria. Let's appoint these five ministers. Should Brkic be on hold for a while. He hasn't been coming to work for a while. I don't know why." Et cetera. These five persons are persons that Izetbegovic wanted to move forward on, did they include the four that you had put forward?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Do you know which of the five, then, that Mr. Izetbegovic wanted to move forward with that wasn't including your four?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly, but I specified the names of the all the ministers on this government with Mr. Izetbegovic, and they were elected unanimously.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if we could then go to - hopefully this time we have it correct - P 10496, which should and record of a meeting -- a meeting of the Presidency the following day, the 179th session. And on the first page or -- well, it would be page 2 not counting the cover pages, page 1, and that should be loose. That document is loose. I assume people have found it by now. There was apparently only one item on the agenda that day and that was "Review of the proposed programme of the RBiH government." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And -- and I can represent to you, sir, in the interests of time and those who are reviewing can review the document, will again I'm sure correct me if I'm wrong, but throughout this document there is again repeat statements of concern about members of the government, members of the Presidency, who were not attending, who were not fulfilling their responsibilities. Do you have any reason to disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that assertion, but there was a war going on. Some people went elsewhere, and other people are very frightened to live under shells in Sarajevo. Both reasons are quite important, especially for some people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. I believe your first intervention in this -- recorded in this meeting is on page 4 of the English version, but if you look down, I think it will be the first time you see your name, and you're quite firm about this, sir. You say: "I will not propose into this government a single person who is absent unjustifiably, and no one will travel for whom the government did not put forward." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said, and I repeat that my government was accepted unanimously.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if you'll skip down to several other interventions by you, you will come to an intervention. It's on page 6 of the English version, about the middle of the page. Mr. Zarko Primorac comes up again and you say: "Zarko Primorac is not in Sarajevo now for three months." So I'm curious. Did you make an exception for Mr. Primorac as someone who could be in the government despite the fact that he had not been present for some substantial period of time, or did you consider Mr. Primorac to be disqualified?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Primorac was not in my government. I talked to him. I proposed to him that he become Minister of Finance. He was not willing to accept that, and therefore he was no longer a candidate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. But above that on the same page there's a statement attributed to a man named Filipovic, and about half -- I'm going to skip the first sentence or two, and Mr. Filipovic represented a group, the opposition parties, if you will, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was one opposition party. I can't give you the exact name, but it was a Muslim party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise, but we want to have the page still on the screen for those who cannot follow, and line 7, page 22, what is recorded is that the witness said -- said "Yes, that's what I said, but I repeat my government had been accepted unanimously." In the original, in the Croatian, he said, "I repeat that my government accepted that unanimously," namely that proposal that only persons who are not absent can join the government, those who are not absent on account of unacceptable reasons. So this is a meaningful difference and perhaps it should be corrected right away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you confirm what Mr. Kovacic just said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, basically I can confirm both. I can confirm that, and I can also confirm that my government was indeed elected unanimously. I don't know what I said out of the two, but both are correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Counsel, for clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just on that point, sir, before we forget and move on. When you say your government was unanimously approved, when is it you say your government was formed, as of when?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give the exact date. The government was formed around that time. I was elected on the 10th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's -- if we can do a little bit better or at least clarify. So when you say "around that time," do you mean in December 1992, January 1993? There's a statement in fact on that point, in this same record, and -- I believe, let me just make sure, maybe it was the previous document, sir. Excuse me a moment. I think it was maybe the previous document, sir, but one of the things that Mr. Izetbegovic says, at one point, I believe it was the previous document, he says: "Forming the government would take at least three months," which if that was the case it would have taken until February, March of 1993. Does that assist you in refreshing your memory about when that might have been?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We establish the government before the new year.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let's go back to Mr. Filipovic, because in the first page of the actual comments not including the cover page, Mr. Izetbegovic introduced in the meeting said that a request had come in. Something had been submitted just immediately prior to the meeting. It's in the fourth paragraph under the word "Izetbegovic." It says: "In fact it's signed by Filipovic, et cetera. In fact, a submission of the united BiH opposition." And then below that it -- Filipovic says: "Yes. I would like to give an explanation about that. " But in the interest of time, sir, would like to then direct your attention back to -- toward the end of the document, on page 6 of the English version, not the last intervention by Mr. Filipovic but I think the third from last, in that paragraph he says: "We should not accept the rule which was here openly proposed, the rule of monopoly of the national parties to represent the people. That we shall not accept. Here it was proposed that that and that party have the exclusive right to propose not only the members and delegate the government members -- and delegate the government members and their Presidency members but even ambassadors. And you concretely have proposed a replacement of the HDZ members as the party vice-president, members, et cetera." And is it correct, sir, that what Mr. Filipovic and the other opposition parties were complaining about or raising issues about is it should not be just to the national parties, that is the HDZ, the SDA, to have say in these matters but all other parties, including minority parties, including members of the opposition, should also be able to participate in that process? Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You certainly know how the opposition functions. Mr. Filipovic was opposition, and there were three parties that were in power and they did not want to let opposition take over.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And there were, in fact, some smaller parties, for example, and parts -- in some parts of the HDZ which may not have agreed with the HDZ's actions or slate of candidates, for example; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is certainly possible, but it is a matter for the political parties involved, not the Presidency. The Presidency functions, and the government functions on the basis of the majority that did exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, let me move forward but staying on the general topic of process, if you will, since we've been told and understand that throughout this period the assembly, the Bosnia-Herzegovina Assembly was not meeting, generally, during this time, and you confirmed that at several points last week when I went back to your testimony. Since the Assembly was not generally in session and you say that you became prime minister around the 10th of November, 1992, by what process were you named or appointed prime minister?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first criterion was for the prime minister to be a Croat, because that was a rule. The Assembly, the Presidency, and the government were always to be led by someone from a different ethnic group. The chairman of the Assembly was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me stop -- let me stop you there for a moment, sir. Excuse me. Let's take it a bit -- bit by bit. So when you say that was rule that in this instance, for example, that the prime minister be a Croat, was this a written rule? Could we find that in the rules of procedure of the Presidency that we looked at a few minutes ago or was it more like it was an understanding, kind of a political understanding?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was the principle in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I didn't say the prime minister had to be a Croat. I said that either the prime minister or the president of the Presidency or the chairman of the Assembly had to be a Croat. Three different ethnic groups, and to each of these belonged one of the three key positions in the country. In this specific case - my apologies - the president of the Presidency was a Muslim, the chairman of the Assembly was a Serb. There was a political agreement in place and this was the established practice as well, and I think even the constitution and nothing else provides for this. It's based on the equal rights of all the three ethnic groups and the contusion clearly says that this must be the way it's done.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, you've now said in the last couple of sentences of the record several different things. It started out being a rule, then it was a principle, and it maybe translation, I'm not -- then it was a political agreement, then it was established practice, and then it was in the constitution. So can you give us a better idea of which one of those it was?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a principle of rotation at the very top level of the government. This rotation took -- had been taking place since --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- had been taken place since 1974 when it came to the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpretation. Sir, again sometimes I'm waiting for the interpretation, and that's why there maybe silence in the courtroom, but that does not always mean that I'm inviting further -- further comment.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But let me again, sir, and I understand that, and you've again said, Well, this was the principle of rotation. But where would we find that? Again, was it just custom and practice? Or it was down in a rule somewhere? Was it in the constitution or not? What is the source of this practice or principle, please?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm what you're asking me to confirm, but this was a golden rule in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It never crossed anyone's mind at any point in time to try to change that or even to doubt the principle. I'm talking about the period before this. I'm not talking about the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go back and apply that specifically to your situation and my original question on this topic. By what process, then, were you name prime minister? Did someone go -- did someone field -- for example I'm not saying this is your answer, I'm trying to give you some concreteness, if I can say that, if you say in this instance it should be a Croat, did someone go to the HDZ? Did someone go to some Croat party and say, Who do you name? Who should be prime minister? Please tell the Judges how -- by what process were you put forward and then confirmed as prime minister?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was nominated by the HDZ, one of the three winning parties. The winning Croat party. Next I talked to the president of the Presidency, who then places this on the agenda, and then the Presidency discusses it. The Presidency nominates me for a term of office, and the Presidency, on behalf of the Assembly, appoints me and bestows upon me the right to be the prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, was that the process because that, as you said a few moments ago, you were operating in wartime conditions or in peacetime? If the Assembly had been -- had been meeting would the process have been different?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing that would have been different is the Assembly would have taken that decision, and here it was the Presidency taking that decision on behalf of the Assembly. The extended Presidency, if you like, or the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So in reality, sir, because of the wartime conditions a number adjustments had been made in the processes followed by the Presidency; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the adjustments were not to be contrary to the contusion. Neither the Assembly nor the Presidency had the power to make any changes to the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I ask you, please, to look next at 1D 01939. It should be in one of the binders. Binder 3. 1D 01939, and I hope we can take this quite quickly. Sir, this appears to be a record of meetings of the Presidency -- a meeting of the Presidency on the 21st and 22nd of June, 1993, and for present purposes I just want to direct your attention immediately to paragraph number 6, and it says: "The Presidency by majority vote did not agree to the proposal that Presidents Izetbegovic and Ganic travel to Sarajevo." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can we take this as an example and can you confirm that even by the summer of 1993 the Presidency was continuing to function on the basis of majority vote?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. Whenever it met, that was principle for their decision-making, and that's precisely what the rules of procedure say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. I would like to turn now to the next topic. And that is the formation of the Croatian Defence Council, the HVO as an armed forces. We've discussed last week, sir, the creation of the new Territorial Defence. When I say "new," I'm not talking about the Territorial Defence as it exist under the former Yugoslavia, which was related to and ultimately controlled by the JNA but the new Territorial Defence of the new State of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You recall talking about that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And that was -- we saw -- once again we looked at the minutes of actions by the Presidency on the 8th and 9th of April, 1992, and I would like for you to look, please -- excuse me a moment. If I could ask you to look, please, at Exhibit P 00151, which should be in the first binder. Do you have that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, hold your finger there, please, and for everyone we're coming right to it, but before I ask you about that document let me -- let me remind you of something that you said in the Kordic case, as we -- as a further introduction to this topic if you will, and for counsel I'm referring to page 20436 of the Kordic transcripts on the 6th of June 2000, 20436. You testified at that time, sir, and I'm going to read it to you, please listen: "The HVO is an armed force that fought against the common enemy. The Presidency believed that all armed forces fighting against aggression are legal and are involved in the state structures for protecting the state. This is also the police. Those are the customs offices and all other bodies. They are even companies that manufacture war equipment. So in that sense the total structure of the defence of the country..." and I'm -- just to be clear I'm injecting the country of Bosnia-Herzegovina. "... includes the HVO as well." Do you confirm and agree with that prior testimony in the Kordic case?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, in Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies. There's something that I would like to say. I went through the documents. There are quite a number of errors there, despite which I entirely agree with my own testimony in the Kordic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, looking now directly at Exhibit P 011 -- excuse me, a moment. 151. Excuse me. This is a decision apparently made by Mate Boban on the -- also on the 8th of April, 1992, the same day as one of the meetings of the BiH presidents that we've now looked at several times, and on the 8th of April, 1992, Mr. Boban as president of the HVO and the HZ HB establishes the Croatian Defence Council as it says here as the "supreme defence body of the Croatian people in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna." Now, do you recall when the creation of the HVO in this way first came to your attention?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was soon after. It wasn't the same day, because I was in Sarajevo, and because the communication channels were not operating, but I was aware of it at the time, and we placed this on the Presidency's agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I would next ask you to go to P 00154, which I hope might be the very next document, but certainly in binder 1. This is a bit longer document. It appears to be on the same general topic, dated the 10th of April, 1992. And if you'll look at the second paragraph of the document, sir, in fact Mr. Boban even makes explicit reference to the action of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina adopted on 8 April 1992, and at the end of that same paragraph Mr. Boban says: "As a result of all this the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna does not accept the compromised TO as its military structure." Now, did that information also come to your attention around that same time as the other item apparently did?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that I haven't seen this before. Nevertheless, you're quite right when you say that he does not accept the TO. He does not accept -- Mr. Boban does not accept the untransformed TO that is still receiving orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. I just wanted to point out, Your Honour, that in order to fully understand that as a result this is not accepted, we must look at the previous sentence, or I would ask that the gentleman look at the entire paragraph thoroughly, particularly the previous sentence where it says, "Even now it speaks sufficiently loudly about the tragedy of the Croatian people and places from Ravno, Neum, and Kupres to Mostar." And I think it -- so we need to look at that in context.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I -- [Interpretation] If I may, I think there's been an oversight. In these questions, there is a suggestion being made there that's just not true. Line 3, at least in the Croatian version, but I think in English, too, it's line 3, there's a explicit reference here to the former TO, the one that up until that point in time had been operating as being in the service of the Serbo-Chetnik armada and so on and so forth. It wasn't about to TO that was soon to emerge as an entirely new force. This is the TO of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. This is an obvious misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said "untransformed," and that is precisely what I had in mind, but Boban is here talking about the Territorial Defence still receiving orders from Belgrade which means from the previous period, and he certainly wasn't talking about this newly established TO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for this clarification. Mr. Scott, you may proceed. It's almost time for the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: How long do you want to -- until how long, Your Honour, do you want to go? It doesn't matter to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can go on until 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Your Honour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that the cafeteria closes just before 4.00. Oh, 5.00 I'm informed. So you can proceed until 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I appreciate all the assistance that we've been given. I simply read the document to you as stated, but the document nonetheless goes on to say below the all in capital letters "Croatian Defence Council" in the middle of the page, Mr. Boban says: "We'll have exclusive Supreme Command of these forces. This body is the only legal one and it's name is the only official one." And then the last paragraph over Mr. Boban's name: "All other military formations on the territory of the HZ of Herceg-Bosna are either illegal or enemy formations." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that, and I think this is also about the former JNA and the paramilitary units that emerged from it later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Isn't it correct, sir, is that the reason -- one of the reasons that Mr. Boban referred to the action of the Presidency dated the 8th of April, 1992, was to also to reject that action then and to continue rejecting it thereafter, that it was not -- would not be recognised on the territory of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think whether the BH army would be recognised in Herceg-Bosna was never something that was questioned, and the same applied the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, we'll let the document speak for itself, but if you can look next at 5D 04271. It should also be in the last binder. 5D 04271. Sir, this appears to be an order by Mate Boban, dated the 10th of April, 1992, the same day, and I would put it to you, sir, that this appears to be implementing the former decision, order, that we looked at a moment ago, Mr. Boban ordering that all Crisis Staffs, all former TO staffs shall be renamed immediately Municipal Staffs of the Croatian Defence Council. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Likewise, in Sarajevo the TO staffs, the all TO staffs were being renamed. Again this is in reference to the old TO, which was Yugoslav in nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, is there some distinction being made that you can tell us about in this document by Mr. Boban between those parts of the TO, the new TO which were under the command of the -- the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina and those new TOs that were under the command of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this was a brief period. It's the 10th of April that we're looking at, isn't it? Therefore, this is two-day period where one simply knew, and it was implicitly recognised that the reference was to the old TO and not the new one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you can look next, and I apologise for again switching around in binders, but I believe we'll be in the first binder for a few minutes after this. If we can go to P 00195, the first binder. P 00195. Sir, this is a -- appears to be an order by General -- colonel-general as described here, and Ante Roso, on behalf of the Croatian Defence Council Main Staff dated the 8th of May, 1992, and the item number 1 is "The only thing legal military units in the territory of the HZ HB are units of the HVO." Now, we've jumped a month forward. You said a moment ago that this was something that -- well, it may have been the case for a day or two or two days, but you confirm, sir, that this was a continuing implementation of Mr. Boban's order that only the HVO were legal military units on the territory of the so-called Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I can give evidence about letters that someone else wrote in areas in which I was not physically present at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, did you know, sir, around this time, as someone who was involved in the Presidency during this time, if not prime minister or someone who had been involved in at that body for a long time, as someone who a few months later became a vice-president of the HDZ, as someone who became the prime minister of this country, that it was the continuing position of the HVO throughout this time that it was the only legal armed force on the territory of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, is this a statement or is this a question? Is he putting this to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Then put it to the witness as a question --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I just did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: "Did you know, sir, around this time," there's a question mark at the end of the sentence if you'll notice. Did you know?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 8th of May, 1992, I was the General-Secretary of the Presidency. I was not a political figure, and I was not vice-president of the HDZ. At the time I was not aware of this, nor indeed was I supposed to be aware of this, nor indeed would I have been under any obligation to be aware of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you ever become aware around this time when you became prime minister, for example, or when you became vice-president of the HDZ, that this had been and was the policy of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again I'm going to object to the form of the question. He is not putting it. If he puts it to the witness he can say, "I put to you that this is what I believe to be the policy. What do you think?" Instead he's putting it as if it is a fact that has already been established as a part of the evidence. It is not fact. It is his case. It's argumentative. It can be argumentative as long as it is put in a -- is phrased in a proper manner. He can put it to the witness as part of a cross-examination but not as an established fact in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, my question is a fair question. He can either say yes or no, I didn't know, it was not, I disagree. I'm just simply asking him what he knew, what he became aware of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Scott, that the objection is justified and you should reformulate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I put it to you, if that will assist, that it was in fact the policy of the HVO throughout this time period, from 1992 into 1993, that the HVO was the only legal armed force that could operate on the territory of Herceg-Bosna. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're putting to me, sir, that is the case, and I'm putting to you, sir, that that is not the case. The HVO was not the only recognised force. When the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which comprised Croats, which comprised members of the HDZ, accepted and agreed a decision for the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina to comprise the BH army, the Croatian Defence Council, and as was said at the time, other defence forces as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you to look at P 00200.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps we can finish this one, Your Honour, before taking the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: P 00200. It should be very close to the document we were just looking at. There is an order by Tihomir Blaskic dated the 11th of May, 1992, again repeating, number one: "The only legal military units in the area of Kiseljak municipality are HVO units." Did you never see any orders like that, sir, or did those items never come up in discussion among the senior leadership of the HDZ or the HVO or Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, this was never discussed at the Presidency. My answer to you is the same as in relation to the previous paper, which means that the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, based on my recollection, never questioned this. As far as I know, it never even reviewed these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, perhaps there's been a misunderstanding. I'm not asking you the position of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina but the -- the policy and position of the Croatian Defence Council and the entity called Herceg-Bosna. Wasn't the position of those bodies throughout this period, as stated here, that the only legal military units operating on the territory of the so-called Herceg-Bosna, the only legal military units for the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, given the point in time we're talking about, I would question Herceg-Bosna as an entity. At least it wasn't an entity in the sense that it is today within the framework of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Secondly, the HVO was a legal armed force, a legal army, recognised by the BH Presidency. It was only a matter of time before a joint command was set up. Eventually one was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you're on your feet?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would ask you to ask the witness to read item 4. Once we've seen that it will become perfectly obvious what the reference is to when we talk about what's legal and what sort of groups and grouplets were working alongside those that were acting independently and what the reference was to when one was saying that those groups should be placed under control. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the English in front of me. All right. I have it in B/C/S as well. Paragraph 4: "I forbid the establishment of private military units. Persons who do not obey this order or fail to carry it out," and I can't see what it says.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note: What the witness has just read makes no sense in B/C/S, therefore we cannot interpret.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Item 5: "By this order, all orders of the TO commander are rendered invalid, and the same is in these areas considered illegal."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we'll have a break. It's five after 4.00, and we will resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, would I like you to look next, please, in the first binder at P 00157. P 00157, article in Vjesnik, or reported Vjesnik dated 11 of April 1992, the title or the headline being "Lumped together in the same basket." And for the English speakers I'd like to go to the top of the second page of the translation. And, sir, if you could find the second paragraph from the bottom of the article, second paragraph from the bottom, and then above that right immediately in the preceding paragraph from the second from the bottom is what I'm talking about. It says: "Also because the decision of the Presidency of B and H has lumped us together in the same basket with all other military and paramilitary organisations and forces existing on the soil of B and H." It goes on to say in the next paragraph: "Asked whether that meant that the Main Staff of the Croatian defence could not accept the decision of the Presidency of B and H of its being put under the command of the Territorial Defence of B and H, Boban stated, 'At this point in time, certainly not?'" Did you become -- were you aware of that statement by Mr. Boban as reported in Vjesnik around this time. Either the statement -- if not the specific statement, the position?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was not aware of it, but let me try and explain his position if that's necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No thank you. My question to you was simply if you were aware of that statement or position. If you weren't, then you weren't. Can I ask you, please, to look next at -- in the third binder 1D 00970. 1D 00970. Third binder. Sir, in that document this refers -- this is an announcement by the Jablanica Municipal Assembly Crisis Staff, dated the 6th of May, 1992, and appears to indicate an effort by Jablanica municipality to unify its defence system into a single armed force consisting of, as stated here, Territorial Defence forces, the Croatian Defence Council, the Green Berets, and all others who wish to place themselves under the unified command of the Territorial Defence headquarters in Jablanica." Now, as someone involved in the Presidency meetings around this time and as later a member of the Presidency, did you become aware or were you aware that there were in fact various municipalities or organisations who or which, as directed by the decision of the Presidency dated the 8th of April, 1992, were attempting to bring all armed forces under a single unified command, including the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember this, but the establishment of joint commands was a continuous process. A lot of argument -- a lot of agreements were signed to that effect, but that process only ended sometime towards the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you look at Exhibit -- in the first binder, binder number 1, Exhibit P 00377. Binder -- sorry, I'm told it's binder 2. Excuse me. Binder 2. My apology. Sir, it appears to me looking over your shoulder, so to speak, that you have that. This appears to be an order by brigadier Milivoj Petkovic, dated the 10th of August, 1992. Item number 1: "You are to use all available HVO civilian and military police forces to prevent any military units other than the HVO from entering your area of responsibility." Can you provide any insight to the Chamber applying the military units of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which by this time were the ABiH, why they would be kept out, off the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I object to this question, because it is never stated in this order that this was indeed an order that relates to the BH army, because at that time the army set up by the BH government was already labelled that. If we look at the municipalities where this order was sent to, we can see that it was in Livno, Tomislavgrad, Posusje, and so on. These are the municipalities with an overwhelming Croatian majority. These are municipalities where there were no BH army units at all. So there is a presumption implicit in my learned friend Mr. Scott's question that has not been proven yet. So in order to clarify this order, perhaps it would be best for Mr. Scott to ascertain whether there were any other units present in those municipalities called the HOS, for instance, or to see in some other way what was the basis for this order. But at any rate, I object to the assumption being made here that this order pertained to the BH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges will consult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber has deliberated and thinks that Mr. Scott is entitled to ask this question. Mr. Scott, you may put your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you provide any assistance the Chamber in explaining why the HVO, and why in particular General Petkovic, would issue an order on the 10th of August, 1992? And the word used is "any," I'll leave the word to speak for itself, any units of the HVO, to prevent any other military units, any including the ABiH from entering territory claimed to be under the command of the HVO? Can you assist us with that or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't really comment on it. I'm not a person who is supposed to provide commentary of other people's letters, but let me repeat once again that the BH army and the HVO did not exclude each other. And I can confirm that there were many paramilitary units, private armies. And I can confirm what Mr. Izetbegovic stated at the beginning of the war, so before this time, that there will be many private, small-scale wars fought within this war. I think that the HVO --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to have to cut you off, sir, and I apologise for that, but we need to move forward. I would like for you to look at Exhibit P 10481. It should be in binder 3. P 10481. If you will turn to -- in the English version it will be page 9. For the -- what is titled a Joint Statement over the names of Tudjman and Izetbegovic. And if you can find that document, sir. Six numbered items in the Croatian version. Sir, in paragraph 3 of that document in the second sentence it says -- and perhaps if -- I can simply read it to you and you can tell me if you can confirm that or not or what comment you care to make about it. "The Republic of Croatia also supports the efforts of the legal government and the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina to consolidate the defence of the republic by uniting all forms and components of armed defence to the unified armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina under the superior command of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Do you understand that to be an accurate statement?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I can't see the signature of President Tudjman, but I think that this is correct, and it is fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I can just quickly ask you because the question of the signatures has come up before, if I can ask you to look also at -- in the same binder 3 a Defence exhibit, 5D 00064. And if you have that, sir. If I can just quickly, please, direct your attention again to paragraph number 3. This appears to be another version reporting what appears to be the identical information, this time on Zagreb Radio Croatia Network on the 15th of June, 1992, and do you see item 3 makes the same statement as the one we looked at a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, would I like to move forward, please, to -- also in the same -- in binder number 3. If you can look at Exhibit P 10190. 10190. It should be the first document in binder 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have yet to hear the question that Mr. Scott wants to ask, but I object to this document being shown to the witness for the same reason that I have already expressed when Mr. Sancevic testified here. This document has already been exhibited. It's admitted into evidence. It's been shown to the witness whose name I will not utter. He was a protected witness, but he was the person best placed to answer questions about this document. It pertains to topics that were not raised in the examination-in-chief, at least as far as we're able to ascertain on the basis of the contents of the document, and I really cannot fathom what connection could be established between the contents of this document and the testimony of the witness so far and the cross-examination by Mr. Scott. At any rate, this is already an exhibit. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, Mr. Coric's Defence is saying that this document has already been admitted, and secondly that it doesn't see the connection between the examination-in-chief, this document and what you have in mind. So could you tell us exactly what you want to elicit from this?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I would like the witness to confirm, Your Honour, a certain individual that's mentioned in the document his role and to confirm that something stated in the document is accurate, and that is the involvement of Mr. Brkic. I think Mr. Brkic's involvement in these matters has come up, has been raised, and it goes to the topic of -- again the same topic that we've been on, among others, and that is the place of the HVO in the -- in or not in the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the recognition or non-recognition of Herceg-Bosna. It's directly relevant to matters that have been discussed with this witness so far.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do apologise, but the person by the name of Brkic is not mentioned in this document that we have under this number.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, perhaps -- if I've misspoken, Your Honour, maybe there's a misunderstanding. I'm talking about P 10190 and as I see his name is mentioned a number of times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: There must and error, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, this is --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sorry, Your Honours. It's been -- my apologies to the Chamber. The number's been -- the document has been mismarked. Perhaps Ms. Winner can assist is me in identifying the document. While that's happening perhaps we can hopefully not lose too much time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Who -- the name Mr. Brkic has come up several times in fact, I believe, including today, Mr. Miljenko Brkic. Who was Mr. Brkic in 1992, and what position, if any, did he hold in any party or political organisation?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miljenko Brkic is a Croat politician from Sarajevo. He is originally from Herzegovina, if that's the person we're talking about. He teaches at the university, and for a while he was the president of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm told, Your Honours, again with my apology, that the proper document is P 10490. P 10490, which still should be in the third binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
