utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I'm told that the gentleman indicated that Mr. Brkic was acting president. It doesn't reflect that in the transcript. Not president but acting president of the HVO. And maybe we can get a confirmation from the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Brkic was the acting president of the HDZ BiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in fact, can you confirm in looking at 1 -- P 10490 that it was at a meeting of the HDZ on the 15th of March, 1992, in Bugojno that Mr. Brkic was elected as the acting president of the HDZ BiH?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did not attend this meeting, but if he was elected, then he was elected. I can't see where the problem is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I didn't suggest there was, sir. I'm just asking if you can confirm -- you confirm then that he was as of spring 1992, then, is it correct, that he was acting president of the HDZ BiH? We're in agreement on that then?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. The document is -- includes the name not only of Mr. Boban but also the name of Mr. Kostroman, who I'm not sure the Chamber has heard much about before. Can you tell the Judges, if you know, what position did Mr. Kostroman hold at that time, and what was his function in the party and in Herceg-Bosna during this time period, the middle of -- spring and middle of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Mr. Kostroman personally. I don't know what position in the party he held at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's described here as the executive secretary and member of the Main Board. Does that seem right to you, or do you have any reason to quarrel with that?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is quite possible. I was in Sarajevo, which was under siege, so I wasn't really in contact with the party, but I have no particular reason to contest this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would you then go to -- and it will be in the first binder, Exhibit P 00312. P 00312. These are the records of a meeting on the -- in particular we look in the second paragraph on the page, on the first page, on the 5th of July, 1992, involving Mr. Tudjman and others. If I can ask you, please, to look at the second page. I believe it will be in both the English and the Croatian versions. I believe it's the first intervention attributed to Mr. Brkic. In the second or third paragraph -- the third paragraph, I believe, it appears to indicate under Mr. Brkic's intervention, he goes on to say: "What is Herceg-Bosna? What kind of association is it? And Posavina, and Central Bosnia also need to be clarified. What is their relationship with the state as whole, what is the HVO? Is this an army or a civilian structure, and what is the scope of its authority? This has not been clarified sufficiently. The HVO has suspended regular civilian authority and even the HDZ." Skipping two paragraphs he goes on to say: "The HDZ party has adopted conclusions and paid tribute to the HVO for what it has done so far, especially regarding free territories. However, the HDZ does not agree with the suspension of civilian authority." Skipping a paragraph, Mr. Brkic says: "By establishing an office in Herceg-Bosna, it provokes a reaction and dilemmas about dual authority and which authority should be obeyed. I must say that some people from Zagreb have been mediating in this, and that I doubt their good intentions -- and that I doubt their good intentions." Now, around this time, mid-1992, do you have any knowledge of Mr. Brkic's views on this topic as stated in this record?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that they put Mr. Brkic -- or, rather, what Mr. Brkic is saying, it's of organisational nature, not political nature. What he means to say is that the Croatian Defence Council should -- should have a completely separate civilian and military segment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: The answer was not very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: One of the statements that I just read to you is a statement by Mr. Brkic that the HDZ does not agree with the suspension of civilian authority. Did you understand Mr. Brkic to have that view?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's possible that it was his personal view, but his statement is erroneous that the HDZ did not agree with it. Perhaps he himself did not agree with this, but the HDZ obviously did agree with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can -- well, Mr. Brkic, sir, at the time was the acting president of the HDZ; correct? You told us a few moments ago.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to say here that the acting president of the HDZ and the president of the HDZ is not the same thing. These posts do not have the same authority. The acting president is there only ad interim, as we would say, and the president of the HDZ has powers vested in him in accordance with the statute that are much broader than the ones that the acting president has.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the president of the HDZ during this time, by the way, that was Stjepan Kljuic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the HDZ used to be Stjepan Kljuic, but at this time when Miljenko Brkic was the acting president of the HDZ, Mr. Kljuic was not the president of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'll put it to you that the very reason, and we looked -- that's why we showed you -- one of the reasons I showed you the minutes of the HDZ meeting in March a few minutes ago, one of the reasons that the HDZ leadership appointed Mr. Brkic as acting president, signed by Mr. Boban and Mr. Kostroman, was that in position and title Mr. Kljuic would remain the president during this time and there was a big fight going on with Mr. Kljuic, wasn't there, and they couldn't get him to resign, so they named Mr. Brkic as the acting president; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to admit that I did not attend those meetings. The interpretation of this text is different, but at any rate, in theoretical and practical terms, if Mr. Brkic was the acting president, then Kljuic was not the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. We won't debate that any longer. There will be other -- there's other evidence on that point, in fact. Can you look, please, at page 3. There's an intervention by Mr. -- someone named V. Baric, and Mr. Baric says: "I think that the very establishment of the HVO was a good thing, but in those places in which the Muslims are in a majority, they do not recognise this because this is a quiet taking over of power." Did you know Mr. Baric?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not Mr. Baric, Mr. Barac, if that is who you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, did you know a person by the name V Barac?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Barac, B-A-R-A-C.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you know a person by the name of V -- first name apparently, V Barac.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him. Not well, but I did know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What position did he hold in July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in the party. I think he's from Zenica. I don't know what he was in the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you say "in the party," do you mean the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the HDZ, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if you go to page 8 of the document, there is an intervention by Mr. P. Juric, and Mr. Juric says: "As regards the conclusions, it is my view that by recognising BH, the legitimately elected authorities in BH should be recognised." Skipping a paragraph he then goes on to say: "It is necessary to clarify somewhat more the activities of Herceg-Bosna, who is financing this and under whose sponsorship it is being done." What position did Mr. Juric hold, if you know, during this time of July 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must admit that I don't know Mr. Juric. Therefore, I don't know whether he was in the party and at what position.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you come to know around this time, sir, that Mr. Boban was having increasing conflict with the leadership of the HDZ party at that time, including Mr. Brkic, people like Jure Pelivan, people like Mr. Barac, people like Mr. Juric? These were people that didn't accept -- they were in the HDZ, and they did not accept the views of Mr. Boban and others. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I was not active in the party. I had my professional job at the Presidency, and I really can not state my views on this. However, I can state my views as follows: Mr. Boban, at a meeting of the Assembly of the party when he was elected president, he was chosen in a very legal way and with a great majority. It wasn't exactly unanimous but there was an overwhelming majority, for sure. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The time that I'm talking about is the time which is -- well, I think October 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, I think we have that document, sir. We can get to that, but let's move forward on my questions at this particular point, please. And if time allows, we may get to that document. During this time Mr. Boban became very annoyed at Mr. Brkic, the people like Mr. Brkic, Mr. Pelivan, and others; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about Brkic but I cannot say that about Pelivan. He wasn't very active in the party so I don't know why Mr. Boban would be annoyed at him. Don't know whether Pelivan was a member of the party at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you to look at page 8 of the document, but in any event, I believe it will be -- if it's not page 8 in the Croatian version, sir, if you can please -- I believe it's the first intervention by someone by the name of Vukojevic. And I believe it's Vice Vukojevic. Can you tell the Judges who Mr. Vukojevic was and what role if any he played at that time in these events?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Vukojevic is a gentleman who originally hails from Herzegovina. At that time lived in Zagreb. He lived -- he would come to Herzegovina. He was a member of the Croatian parliament. And I don't know whether he finished his career this way or not, but he was at any rate a Judge on the Constitutional Court of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you know why he Mr. Vukojevic would attend a meeting with President Tudjman with various leadership of the HDZ from Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can just give you my opinion. I did not attend -- I did not invite him to meetings. I don't know whether he did attend the meetings that I attended, but I think that what is of relevance is his origins.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter cannot hear the witness because of background noise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apology. It was probably my fault.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, are you saying that because the man was from -- was from Herzegovina that entitled him to attend a president -- a meeting with President Tudjman and the Bosnian Croat leadership?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that that is the case, that he was invited in that sense, because he was familiar with the subject matter of Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I've already said that I don't know the reasons why he was asked and who invited him. I can just make an assumption, but I don't know the specific reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Isn't it correct, sir, that Mr. Vukojevic was one of the confidantes of President Tudjman, that together with Mr. Susak was one of the persons most directly involved in the matters involving Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: President Tudjman and Mr. Vukojevic, I'm not aware of their relationship and what it was like, so whatever you are saying is your own words. It is not any recognition on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Going to page 7 of the document, again to Mr. Brkic, there's a reference to an intervention by Mr. Brkic on the topic -- he says, "...the attitude towards the BH government." And he says, "If you recognise BH it is logical to recognise the government." Do you --

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I can't find it. Mr. Brkic; right. Oh, yes, I have found it, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If says: "If you recognise BH, it is logical to recognise the government." Is that a true statement, an accurate statement? That is the substance of it? I don't mean -- do you see that he makes it. Do you agree with the content of that statement and the position expressed that if one was to recognise Bosnia-Herzegovina as a sovereign, independent state, it is logical to follow from that that you recognise the government of that state, or did you have a different view?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, in the Croatian text what is stated is that there is a recognition of authority. Authority is not only the government. That is a far broader concept than the government as such. So I assume that Mr. Brkic is saying here if the BH is being recognised, it is logical to recognise the government or authority. That is only natural.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At page 10 of the document above -- if you can find first as a landmark, if you will, above as part of the page where it says "Conclusions," there are some statements attributed to Mr. Manolic. And it says: "Mr. Manolic maintains that Mr. Brkic and Mr. Boban should show more restraint their communication and should consult each other as much as possible. They should meet more often and solve problems. The HDZ party is above the HVO and the civilian authorities. Transitional organs of power can be established where the authorities have been destroyed. Legally elected authorities must not be disturbed. The HVO cannot be in charge of the civilian authorities." Were you ever aware of that position being taken or expressed by Mr. Manolic? Because there were occasions where you were in meetings with Mr. Manolic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did attend some meetings, and I can explain what this was all about. Some people thought, Mr. Manolic included, that wherever war conditions allowed the government elected by the people could and should function, that is to say through deputies in the BH Assembly. I think that this is a position within the HVO as was also taken by the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that when there was a state of war and an imminent threat of war assemblies cannot be held of the legal organs of the government and then the HVO replaces them just like in Sarajevo the government replaced the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, the difference being the members of the Presidency were elected to those positions, at least most of them, as we discussed last week, whereas the members of the HVO were not elected; correct? And if you can point me, sir, to any time that there was an election held in the territory claimed by Herceg-Bosna during the time 1992, 1993, in which any persons were elected to the HVO government, please -- please tell us when that happened?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot talk about that. I don't know how the HVO functioned. I don't know that in any detail. But I know that Herceg-Bosna was established -- or, rather, those deputies who won the largest number of votes in their respective municipalities established it. I am referring to the elections for the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It was the -- if I can have the assistance of the usher. This is one of your statements in the testimony in Kordic I would like to put to you. Hopefully the ELMO is working today. Put that on the ELMO, please. This comes from the page -- the transcript in Kordic 20434, line 19. If you can enlarge that perhaps a little bit, please. Sir, you testified in the Kordic case: "The general position of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina was that the establishment of the HVO was quite legal, and that the establishment of the Community of Municipalities of Eastern Bosnia and the establishment of the Croat community of Herceg-Bosna was illegal." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I was talking about the positions within the Presidency. However, the Presidency itself did not make such a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, that was your testimony under oath in the Kordic case correct, that the general position of the Presidency in Bosnia and Herzegovina, you didn't say any individuals, you said the Presidency, was that the establishment of the Croat community of Herceg-Bosna was illegal; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wish to say once again that general positions taken by the Presidency are not one and the same thing. This is a conversation within the Presidency that was not turned into conclusions of the Presidency. That was my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'd like you to next go, please, in the first binder, it should be the last document in binder 1, P 00336. Sir, this is a record of a meeting a few weeks later after the meeting that we looked at a moment ago with Mr. Brkic and others on the 5th -- excuse me, I believe on the 12th -- no, on the 5th of July, 1992. This is on the 21st of July, 1992, and there are just a few similar statements made in this record that I would like to ask you about. If you can turn, please, sir, the pages in this document should be identical in either the English or the Croatian versions. So if I tell you page 59, for example, you should be able to find -- it should be the same page 59 in both versions. And indeed I would like you to turn to page 59.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am going to look at the English version like the one that you have, because I can't really find this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's up to you, sir. As I said, the pages should be identical in the Croatian version as well. Sir, on page -- starting on page 59 there are statements by President Tudjman. He refers to Mr. Izetbegovic and then he says: "That the both -- that both delegations agree that the status of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina should be on the basis of three constitutive units in Bosnia-Herzegovina," that is the first thing. Then going over to page 60, and second that "the defence forces of the Croatian Defence Council are considered to be an integral part of the defence forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that they are to be represented in the command, the joint command of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Do you see that, please?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And go down page -- down page 60 to Mr. Izetbegovic,

utterances.speaker: MR. IZETBEGOVIC SAYS
utterances.text: "The second thing is not only acceptable but it is also necessary and of course desirable in all ways, the second being the reference to the HVO as an integral part of the Defence forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Then Mr. Izetbegovic goes on to say: "As for the first thing, we wouldn't want to prejudice that issue." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you know that to be -- both of these statements to be consistent with the position taken by Mr. Izetbegovic during this time, mid-1992, on both of those topics; that is, that he did indeed recognise the HVO as an integral part of the -- excuse me, of the defence forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that on the other hand did not accept at this time, at least in this meeting, the division of Bosnia into three separate ethnic states? Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At any rate it is correct that Mr. Izetbegovic recognised the HVO, and it is correct that it -- that he recognised the three constituent peoples. As for three ethic units, he was very suspicious about that. Ultimately he accepted that, too, but it never happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you ever know anyone named -- involved in maybe higher levels of the Croatian government or the HVO or the HDZ called Mr. Milan Gromiljak?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew the gentleman. He was deputy prime minister of Croatia. Originally he also hailed from Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is what I wish to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask you to go to page 150 -- 152 of the record, of the transcript. Page 152. And Mr. Ramljak says on this page he's talking about again some of the organisational matters referring to the people -- the dialogue with the people from the Croatian Defence Council, and that's the main subject here, the armed component is to be put immediately under the command. Then while he goes on to -- while this component is getting adjusted as the circumstances allow. Now, did you understand during this time, sir, that it was the position of Mr. Izetbegovic that while he recognised the HVO as an integral part of the armed forces of the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that was only so to the extent that it subordinated itself to a unified command of the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the word that you used, "subordinate," is not appropriate. The appropriate term there would be that all armed forces be subordinated to a Joint Command that would have as its Supreme Commander the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, that's exactly my question to you, sir. An armed forces, it was legal -- Mr. Izetbegovic accepted the legitimacy or legality of the HVO so far as it recognised and put itself under the command of the BiH Presidency; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He recognised the HVO without any further assumptions or without pre-judging anything, and further assumptions -- or, rather, requirements are agreements on a Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, perhaps we misunderstood each other, but a moment ago you testified on page 59 that "the appropriate term there would be all armed forces would be subordinated to a Joint Command that would have as its Supreme Commander of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina"; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, but you are asking me questions in different ways, and I cannot answer them all the same way. It is correct that Mr. Izetbegovic recognised the HVO. Well, not Mr. Izetbegovic. It's not his affair, but it was the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina that did, recognised the Presidency, recognised the HVO as one of the segments of the armed forces of the BH. It is correct that talks were under way in order to establish and a Joint Command between the HVO and the BH army. It is also correct that in that case the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina would be the Supreme Commander of the armed forces as enshrined in the constitution. What I'm saying here is the Presidency with its full legitimacy. However, this is not what we are discussing at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you will go then to page 144 of the record, transcript. On the bottom of that page we have again an intervention by the same Mr. Miljenko Brkic. "Mr. President, when the HVO appears as a military structure, then the Muslims and Croats are united, but at the moment when the HVO appears as a civilian structure, then the Muslims don't accept it in the entire area of the central Bosnia-Herzegovina." Again, did you understand that and going back to the previous document that we were looking at, did you understand that to be the position of Mr. Brkic, the acting president of the HVO BiH at this time, that while the HVO was accepted as a military structure to the extent that it was subordinate to the BiH Presidency, it did not accept the HVO as a civilian authority?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Obviously that's what Mr. Brkic stated here by way of his own position.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would you go, please, to page 149 of the transcript. This is a continuing discussion. People can look at previous pages if they wish, 148 and following, of the nature and character of the HVO as a civilian government. At the top of page 149 Izetbegovic refers to -- talks something called its civilian government, and do you see in the middle of that page that Mr. Pelivan says: "This will not pass in the government. I know the members of the government." Tudjman: "It won't pass in which government? Pelivan: "In the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Wasn't Mr. Pelivan making it very clear to this government together with Mr. Izetbegovic that the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina would not accept a position recognising Herceg-Bosna as a political authority -- or civilian authority in parallel to the BiH state?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I have to say here is my own view, that the civilian authority of the HVO is not parallel. It is not parallel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's not my question, and you have to answer my question at this point, please, if you can. If you don't know, say you don't know. Wasn't it the position of Mr. Pelivan and Mr. Izetbegovic, as expressed in this meeting, and was it familiar -- was it a point known to you at the time that there was a rejection of the HVO as a civilian or governmental authority as opposed to, as distinct from, the HVO as a military component of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina? I'm not asking your personal views, sir. I'm asking were you aware of the fact that Mr. Pelivan and Mr. Izetbegovic took that -- those positions during the middle of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is also what Mr. Pelivan is assuming here. So he's assuming, and I can assume too. Mr. Pelivan said this will not get through the government. I know what the composition of the government is. He didn't say this was the adopted by the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Pelivan was the prime minister in July -- of Bosnia-Herzegovina in July 1992; correct? He was the prime minister before you. And Mr. Pelivan is the prime minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina was making it very clear to Tudjman and all those present that the acceptance of Herceg-Bosna as a legal or legitimate political or civilian government would not be accepted, was not acceptable; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, this has to do with the civilian part of the HVO. Mr. Pelivan -- well, I have to say this. Mr. Pelivan said, "I know what the composition of the government is like." That is to say that the Muslim members of the government prevailed, had a majority in the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's speculation on your part, sir. I'm simply asking you whether what Mr. Pelivan -- excuse me. I don't think that's appropriate at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, what Mr. Pelivan said was this would not be accepted by the government, and then on page 150 -- in the middle of page 50 he goes on to say, "The fact is that this may cause disapproval on the other side. Serbs will also request to have their government." And the meaning I put it to you, sir, that if this was -- if the legitimacy of Herceg-Bosna was recognised, then it would be no difference in recognising the Serb entity as equally legitimate; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the position of Mr. Pelivan. I don't want to go into that debate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if you are going to -- if we are going to stay with this topic, I also suggest that the gentleman be given an opportunity to look at page 151 where Dr. Franjo Tudjman voices his opinion in the context of this entire discussion and that's what we're having. We're having a discussion here and I think it's -- but frankly I think we're asking the gentleman to opine about a situation where he wasn't a participate to the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, two responses to that. As to looking at the entire -- the rest of the transcript, the entire transcript is admitted into evidence and of course the Chamber has that in front of. If Mr. Karnavas would like to pursue it on redirect, certainly he can do that. Secondly, this is a man who was involved in one capacity or another in the most senior levels of the government and Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I am putting to him what I suggest, what I submit to the Court, are fundamental positions of the parties during this time, fundamental positions. And if Mr. -- I don't know if he's telling us this, I haven't heard him say this myself I don't think, but if Mr. Akmadzic is telling us that he had no knowledge about the respective positions of various parties to these ongoing negotiations, then I would question his entire foundation of his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour. Your Honour, I don't want to prolong the situation. Obviously Mr. Scott was not listening to the direct examination. He was rather clear about what the positions were of the respective parties, Mr. Izetbegovic, Silajdzic, all those who are participating on the Muslim side, the Croat side, the Serb side. So I don't know why we're attacking the credibility of the witness at this point. Now he's asking him to give an opinion about what Mr. Pelivan thought. Those were Mr. Pelivan's opinions and we can read them. But I don't know what's trying to accomplish with this cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm trying to get him to confirm, Your Honour, and I think I'm entitled to attempt to do so, that contrary to the difference in what Mr. Karnavas just said and the position that I'm arguing, it's the point that I'm putting to the witness at this point is that it wasn't just Izetbegovic and the Muslims who disagreed. It was senior members on the Croat side with acting president of the political party Mr. Brkic who was elected, who was duly elected as acting president in March 1992, I put that document in front of the Chamber, and Mr. Pelivan who was the prime minister, the Croat prime minister of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time, so it's not just to say all of this -- these were just Mr. Izetbegovic's positions. These were positions by senior Croats as well who obviously rejected the position of Mr. Boban and others like him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm clearly entitled to put that to put this point to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We can see that there were various positions taken. We also know from the previous witness that Mr. Brkic had his own ideas as far as what he thought the internal make-up should be. So that's -- this has never been an issue that people had different positions. I don't see what the dilemma is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you would like to confront the witness with Mr. Pelivan's position as expressed on -- in this document on page 150. You'd like the witness to confirm that or not. The witness seems to state that what Mr. Pelivan said was his responsibility. The witness was not present. He was not for or against it. During redirect Mr. Karnavas may ask questions on the matter. You may proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask you to -- if I can ask you, please, to go to the third binder, to Exhibit 1D 00507. 1D 00507. And sir, this appears to be a decree on amendments of the decree with the law on the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and on the action taken on the 6th of August, 1992, so a very short time after the meeting in Zagreb on the 21st of July. And do you recognise this, sir, as action taken by the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina implementing, in fact, further, as stated in Article 1, that the integral -- that the armed force of the republic is consisted -- or consists of, the translation may be a bit rough, consists of the army of the republic, hereafter referred to as army, the integral parts of the army are formed of the Croatian Defence Council as well as the other armed groups which are put under the united command of the army. Now, wasn't this an action duly taken by the Presidency on the 6th of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but there's an error here if I may point it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It reads: "The armed forces of the republic comprise the army of the republic henceforth the army. The army comprises units of the Croatian Defence Council as well as a component of the army." This is an error, because obviously what is meant here is a component of the armed forces and not a component of the army. If you look at all the material that we've gone through so far that is the own conclusion that you can draw.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I take it -- I understand that's your -- you argue that. I'm just simply saying what the document says on its face. Sir, you may want to argue a different point now. But nonetheless, you confirm that that was a legitimate action taken by the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Let me ask you to please to look next at the same binder 3, 1D 02432. Sir, this is an order dated the 16th of October, 1992, which the Chamber has seen before, an order issued to the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina (the BH army and the HVO). And according to what you've told us so far, sir, and I would understand you to say that this is a completely legal order, correct? Recognising both of the -- giving order to both components of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. However, if you look at paragraph 2 or item 2, sir, you see Jasmin Jaganjac is appointed commander of the operation with full powers, and Mirsad Catic his deputy. Other members of the operation are Zejnil Delalic and Ferid Buljubabic. All of them are Muslims. I think this order, this operation, is something that the Presidency never adopted. If you look further up the page you see the BH Presidency, the president's office. This is not an order that invokes a Presidency decision, and Mr. Izetbegovic here --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I object. I object. He is and entitled to complete his answer because we know from the prior testimony that it is the Presidency that is the Supreme Commander and not Izetbegovic, and here we see Izetbegovic usurping the powers of the Presidency, acting as a dictator in a sense, and that is what we have been maintaining all along; that at some point he began acting as if he was the head of a state. And he's entitled to his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My question was to the witness, I am trying to go back and clarify the record, because the witness just a few moments ago said, in answer to my question, "Is that a completely legal order," and the answer at page 16 -- excuse me, page 66, line 16, is "Yes. It is a completely legal order." Now, whether the make-up of the officers who were appointed in paragraph number 2 and further comment he may wish to make that, but I'm simply accepting the witnesses answer that he gave to us, and the document can be argued beyond that. It is titled at the top of the page "The Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina Office of the President." It has Mr. Izetbegovic's signature on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I demand that the witness be allowed to answer the question that was posed to him. He was in the process of answering the question and I see no reason why we should be cutting off the individual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, what did he want to say? Please finish your answer when you were cut off allegedly. What did you want to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what I wished to tell the Honourable Chamber: I recognise Mr. Izetbegovic's signature here. That is beyond dispute. There are two things, however, that are subject to challenge. Mr. Izetbegovic is not adopting this based on a Presidency conclusion or decision. It's something that he chooses to do himself independently. How can we tell? Two things. One, the heading says, "The president's Office" and not "The Presidency." Two, just ahead of the order in this document he does not invoke any Presidency decision. He says if necessary and puts in this as he sees fit. Just last Friday I told the Honourable Chamber that any Presidency decisions were signed by the president, but he must then invoke those. What we see here is the president signing on his own behalf without invoking any Presidency decisions simply because there was none to the effect. The other thing, paragraph 2, if you look at the appointment, it is clear that the Presidency would never have adopted a decision like that, because all the appointments were Muslim appointments. The Croats or the Serbs in the Presidency would never have played along with something like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, what you're saying is your opinion. Of course you're entitled to say this. But what I'm interested in is the following. It's the question of HVO. Let's put Izetbegovic on the side, but did the Presidency recognise the HVO as the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The Presidency recognised the HVO as one of the two key components of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Second question: This document and this document -- your answer seems to go in that direction, but the HVO is recognised as an armed forces. Now, I'm wondering whether the Presidency recognised that the HVO could have a civilian role. Answer by yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say yes or no simply because the Presidency never discussed this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was never discussed within the Presidency? Never, ever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. At least that's clear. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, just to follow up on the president's question. Putting aside Mr. Izetbegovic at this particular moment, but just as a point of principle, based on what you've testified to so far is it correct, though, that the president of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as the Supreme Commander of the armed forces of the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina, could give legal orders to both the of the army -- what's called the ABiH and the HVO? Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in keeping with what we have pointed out already. The Presidency comprised the three groups, and all the three groups had to be involved in the decision-making process.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's your argument and position. I understand that. But the point is that the Presidency was the Supreme Commander of all armed --- excuse me, sir, the Presidency was the Supreme Command -- you've said it several times, and I want to make sure that we're not saying different things here, the Presidency was the Supreme Commander of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina including the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well Your Honour before the witness answers.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: I'm sure my learned friend means nothing by it, but it does have the unfortunate effect of coming across in a slightly pejorative manner, that the witness of course is not making an argument. He is giving testimony under oath, and on a number of occasions my learned friend has perhaps fallen into error, or by complete inadvertence, by seeking to categorise the witness's evidence as an argument. I think that's rather unfair and I'm sure that it was not intended.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My question stands, sir. The Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina was the Supreme Commander of all legal armed forces, if they were legal, it was the Supreme Commander of all armed forces of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina and any orders that it issued to the HVO would be a legal order and would be binding on the HVO. Is that your position? Or was the HVO entitled to pick and choose which orders it would follow and which ones it would not?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The HVO was not entitled to that. Just today I read back for your benefit the rules of procedure of the president, the decisions of the Presidency are legal as long, and we must never tire of pointing this out, as they were made in keeping with the rules of procedure. What this means is this: Military decisions to do with defence had to be adopted by consensus or with a minimum of five votes in favour. The rules of procedure make this perfectly clear. This is not something that I am suggesting. It's a matter of regulations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: While Mr. Scott remains silent, Witness, I think you might be mingling two issues. The question as I understand it is a rather abstract question. Suppose that there is a legal order by the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which is a supposition. Is the HVO -- was the HVO obliged to follow such an order? Your answer, however, went directly to the legality of the order. You changed the premise of the question and says, "At that time there were no legal orders." That may well be the case. I do not think that this was covered by this question. This question makes a supposition which you say is not realistic. Never mind. If there had been an order completely legal, all formalities required, all members needed present and taking part and a clean majority of the Presidency, would then the HVO have been obliged to follow such an order or not? I think that -- that was mainly the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but there would have been a commitment, and the commitment would have been to set up a Joint Command, because that, too, was enshrined in the Presidency decision. My answer to you at any rate is yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, this Joint Command, this is very important also. This is a question I've already put to you, but I would like everything to be clear. In your mind this Joint Command, does it mean that it should comprise the Serbs, the Croats, and the Muslims, or does the Joint Command mean that there should be a head from whichever ethnical ethnicity, and the rest would be whatever? So what exactly is this Joint Command? In the military there can't be all sorts of heads. There has to be one Supreme Commander and then there is a hierarchy in the chain of command. So what do you mean exactly when you said there had to be a Joint Command? In Article 2 for example, in this document, I was wondering if the Presidency had adopted this text, Article 1 would not have changed and then Article -- Article 1 would not have chained and Article 2 maybe Jasmin Jaganjac would have been appointed commander of the operation and they would have had, maybe, a Serb and a Croat deputy. So could you please define what for you is a Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in this specific case we are looking at Sarajevo's deblockade. Sarajevo had been under siege by the Serb army. Therefore, they were not part of the Joint Command. I'm talking off the top of my head because I'm not a military expert. Joint Command might have five members or perhaps seven as the Presidency. One of them is at the head. That's my understanding. However, any key decisions are taken jointly, whereas the Presidency is the Supreme Commander, as a civilian body none of us in the Presidency were a general, a lieutenant, a colonel, or anything like that. We were all civilians. We were not experts in warfare, but we knew about politics, or at least that was the assumption. In an operative sense an army is under the command of a Joint Command, under the command and control of a Joint Command, in this case comprising members of the HVO and the BH army. I think there is a command like that these days in Bosnia and Herzegovina comprising three components involving the army of Republika Srpska. Therefore, the system is quite a complex one. Nevertheless we were three peoples and unless there was to be an all-out war, everyone against everyone one else, we had to reach some sort of an agreement as to how to get along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's clear. I understand you. Mr. Scott. I'm looking at the clock. Time flies here, but maybe we need to have a break. Twenty-minute break, and we'll resume at 10 after 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, just to finish up on this sequence of events before turning to a different topic, just to confirm again then your testimonies to date, it's correct, is it not, sir, that it was then in the fall of 1992 that Mr. Brkic was removed or no longer the acting president of the HDZ BiH; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not correct. Mr. Brkic was not removed. He was not re-elected. He had decided not to run to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. He -- I think -- I think we have some other documentation on that. And he was replaced, correct, finally in -- at an Assembly of the HDZ BiH in, I believe October or -- I think November of 1992. He was replaced finally once for all by Mate Boban as president of the party; correct? Mr. Boban became the president of the HDZ BiH in November 1992. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that he did not replace Mr. Brkic, and he didn't become the president. He was elected according to party procedures. He was elected president.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir. Sir, time is short and I don't want to mince too many words with you. As of November 1992, Mr. Brkic was no longer acting president of the HDZ BiH, and Mate Boban was the president of the HDZ BiH; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And likewise, by the fall, approximately October 1992, is the date that I think you indicated to us yesterday, that by approximately October 1992 Mr. Pelivan was no longer the prime minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was in November.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And after Mr. Pelivan was no longer prime minister of Bosnia and Herzegovina in October or November 1992, you became the -- the prime minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You were elected at an HDZ Assembly in November 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not correct. I wasn't elected at an HDZ Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apologies, sir. You're absolutely correct. You became in 1992 at an HDZ Assembly you were named on the -- on the nomination of Mate Boban the vice-president of the HDZ BiH; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then around that same period of time you then were made or named prime minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to the topic of the peace negotiations which you spent a fair amount of time talking about, and I guess the basic proposition I want to explore with you, sir, I put to you is that there were a lot of negotiations. There were lots of talks, but until Washington -- until the Washington agreement was signed in February or March 1994, there was never any final agreement that was actually implemented; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was never a full implementation, but there were some other changes in terms of organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, I don't know how it translated into Croatian, but in the English language we have a saying about things that -- it's probably not politically correct to say this any more, I suppose, but it's not over until the fat lady sings. Ever heard that?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had another expression. We would say this: It's not over until it's cut and dried.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I take that one as well. And just touching on a few of these various negotiation processes, if you will. I think you said earlier, and I'm not sure we need to take the time to look at it, but I think it was shown to you during direct examination. I'll just mention it for the record. I'm not suggesting we go there unless someone in the courtroom insists, in 1D 02438, I believe we looked at a letter that you wrote to Susak on the 21st of May, 1992, forwarding some information for Mr. Brkic in connection with the Cutileiro negotiations. Is that true? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you just assist us with -- how -- why did you think that by sending the information to -- that Mr. Susak was the appropriate person to send that information to, that if you sent it to Mr. Susak it would get to Mr. Brkic?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We see here the 21st of May, 1992. Mr. Brkic left Sarajevo on or about the 1st of May. This was a technical issue: What was the most convenient way for me to forward my letter to Mr. Brkic. At the time, at least as far as I knew, he was in Zagreb. I assumed that he was in touch with Mr. Susak. I had Mr. Susak's address, but I did not have Mr. Brkic's address. This is a purely technical issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And it's correct, is it not, that in connection with the Cutileiro negotiations that the Croats, in fact, rejected the map put forward by the European Community, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croats never rejected any plan, and the same applied to the Cutileiro Plan. The Croats accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you look please at P 09927, which should be in the last binder -- last document in the second binder. And I believe, sir, that there should be available there to you a translation of the excerpt that I'm -- in Croatian that I'm going to put to you. Sir, if you can look at P 09927, on page 112 of the of English version, and as I said I believe you'll find attached a Croatian translation of the part that I'm going to put to you, on the approximately -- a little below the middle of that page if you refer by reference to footnote 222, it says: "The Croats were the first to repudiate the EC map publicly. Miljenko Brkic, several days after agreeing to the Cutileiro Plan, insisted that cantonal borders would have to be redrawn -- have to be drawn," excuse me, "on the basis of the 1961 census." That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And toward the end of that page, and it isn't in the -- forgive me, but it isn't in the translated portion, but if you can assist us, in that same paragraph with reference to footnote 228, it says: "A group of 93 Croat intellectuals from Bosnia criticised the EC plan, asserting that it was contrary to results of the referendum on independence and that 59 per cent of the Croats in Bosnia would become national minorities if Cutileiro's map were adopted." Do you recall a statement being issued around this time, the end of March 1992, by a group of something like 93 Croat intellectuals?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find the portion that you quote, but I understand your question. I think I can answer it regardless of not having found the appropriate portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you can, please.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the group that you specified. I know of intellectuals who did not agree with the Cutileiro Plan. The Cutileiro Plan had three variants, as it were. These intellectuals, I think, repudiated the variant in which Bosnia and Herzegovina was supposed to be carved up into three parts in order to form a confederacy. The Sarajevo intellectuals specifically, because I was in Sarajevo, repudiated that particular idea. They came to see me. I was not, myself, involved in the negotiations, but I lent them an ear. [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sorry to interrupt you. I thought you were finished. Sorry. Now -- but the bottom line, sir, as I said a few moments ago, that whatever all the negotiations were, there was never a final signed, agreed, implemented Cutileiro Plan; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing was signed, that's true, but some of the principles enshrined in the plan were accepted by both the Serbs and the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in fact, sir, in terms of these negotiations, was there virtually any time between 1991 and 1995 that there wasn't some peace negotiation going on somewhere? Whether it was the Vance Plan or Cutileiro or Vance Owen or Owen Stoltenberg or Washington Agreement, isn't it true, sir, that throughout this period there were ongoing negotiations of one sort or another, none of which led to an actual final agreement until the Washington Agreement; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that the negotiations were ongoing. It is true that eventually all three parties and the international community, as well as the Security Council, accepted the principles along which Bosnia and Herzegovina should be organised. All the negotiations to follow were to be focusing on those principles. I think you know the principles, and I think the Chamber is well aware of these principles. I don't know them by heart but there were a total of nine principles, the first one being --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to cut you off. I'm sorry that I have to do that. If we had time we could talk about this at greater length, and I'd certainly additional questions to you for that matter as well, but we don't. And moving on from Cutileiro, sir, the Vance-Owen process eventually died without any final agreement or implementation. It was never accepted by the Serbs, among other things; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All they parties accepted the Vance-Owen Plan. First in Geneva, the nine principles, and the military agreement --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in May of 1993 the Serb Assembly rejected the Vance-Owen Plan; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The principle for these negotiations was this: Following the negotiations there would be a constitution that --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, the Serb Assembly in May 1992 rejected the Vance-Owen Plan; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. But then it was signed by their legal representatives on the 2nd of May in Athens, the 2 of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it correct, sir, do you recall that it was in June 1993, as a result of additional negotiations between Milosevic and Tudjman, that there was an another plan presented, what became a plan or -- by some to again divide Bosnia and Herzegovina into three ethnic states?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that this was a result of negotiations between Milosevic and Tudjman, but I know that it was a result of a proposal sent to us from the negotiations involving Owen and Stoltenberg and it is normally referred to as the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's correct, is it not, that Mr. Vance resigned as the UN's negotiator in May 1993, and it was proposal of talks resulting from talks between Milosevic and Tudjman which were then put to Owen and Stoltenberg in June of 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm unable to confirm this. I don't, however, think that this is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall at any time in these ongoing negotiations at one time or another after the middle of May -- excuse me, after the middle of 1993 discussions that included the concept that once Croatia and Serbia had sorted out their own relations between the two of them, that Croatia, Serbia, and this newly restructured Bosnia-Herzegovina could engage in a further three-way exchange of territories? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. I think the question is rather vague. Who is having these discussions, and can we -- can we see some documentation concerning this?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Discussions were representatives of the Croats and Serbs, and if you remember -- do you remember that, sir, or not?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A brief answer would be no. I don't remember the talks. I was not aware of that kind of talks going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And again by early 1994, Owen-Stoltenberg process ended without any final agreement; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in fact, in effect or what actually happened was that the Washington Agreement displaced or came in and, if you will, bumped what was then being called Owen-Stoltenberg off the table, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In connection with the negotiations, sir, there's one particular time period that I would like to ask you about now, and that is during the ongoing talks involving the Vance-Owen process in January of 1993, and I would like you to look in that regard at Exhibit P 01146, which should be in the second binder, P 01146. Excuse me? Second binder? Yes. Sir, if you look -- if you have that document, this is a document that the Chamber has seen before that -- it's a decision issued by Jadranko Prlic on the 15th of January, 1993, and it starts off by saying: "In accordance with the agreements so far reached and signed at the International Conference," et cetera, "in Geneva," and then gives a decision involving six points below that. And, sir, I put it to you, you know, don't you, that the statement at the beginning of that document, "In accordance with the agreements so far reached and signed," there were as of the 15th of January, 1993, there were no agreements reached and signed to implement the Vance-Owen Plan, were there?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not signed completely, but partially, yes. In this specific case, I've already said that the military agreement on the 4th of January was reached but not signed. It was definitely to be applied when the entire agreement was to be signed. However, our negotiators, or, rather, the co-chairmen preferred implementation of the agreement when possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, this was a -- this decision and others that flowed from it, this was an entirely unilateral act by the HVO not supported by the Vance-Owen negotiations as they existed at that time; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This decision was in accordance with the negotiations, but the negotiations hadn't been finished yet. This decision, if we look at it as an objective, not a means, implies the establishment of a Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So you mean that the HVO in issuing this decision was looking into the future in the crystal ball and seeing that there would eventually be an agreement, and based on that they were saying they should go ahead and implement it now. Is that what you're telling us? My question to you, sir, was: On the 15th of January, 1993, given the then-existing Vance-Owen negotiations, there was no such agreement, there were no final agreements, and this order and others like it was the completely unilateral order of the HVO; correct? The fat lady hadn't sang yet, had she?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that at that time precisely on the 15th of January, I think, there was a meeting between Boban and Izetbegovic in Zagreb. I did not attend the meeting, so I cannot -- or, rather, I don't know what it was that they had agreed upon, whether they agreed to establish a Joint Command as well and to have military forces withdrawn into the provinces as agreed or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So everything you just said was pure speculation, then, based on what you just told us. You don't know. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be sure, but I know that the military agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... "I cannot -- or, rather, I don't know what it was that they had agreed upon." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between Boban and Izetbegovic I don't know what was agreed, but I know what was agreed in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, again with the help the usher I would like to put before your -- some testimony from the Kordic case. And for counsel it's page 20468, 20468 on the 6th of June, 2000. And again, there's a Croatian translation of that part again to assist you.

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's not what I'm looking at. We haven't got the right ... no, sorry. We're not getting the ELMO. We're getting e-court. There it is. Sir, did you not testify in the Kordic case under oath in June 2000 in response to this question the following: "This order in January 1993 is a unilateral HVO order and in the relevant provinces it subjugates the Muslim Territorial Defence to the HVO; correct? "Answer: Yes. What you just said is correct? "Question: And in terms of legality it does so without legality? "Answer: There was not part of the entire agreement between the Croat and Bosniak sides. At least I do not know of this having been agreed with the Bosniak side or of the BH army." Now, that's what you testified to under oath in the Kordic case, being correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's correct, and I think that I said today that I was not aware of an agreement. If I'm not aware of an agreement and if there was an agreement then it's a one-sided thing; however, I was under oath then and I am under oath today and I state that was not aware of any agreement. I stated then and I state today that the military -- that the military agreement --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, beyond any speculation that you want to engage now, what your testimony is and it's clear from everything you know, not what you speculate about, but what you know, as you said in Kordic and as you -- isn't it true that as you say today this was a unilateral HVO order that was completely illegal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection. Objection. Now, we have the Prosecutor testifying and taking liberties. The gentleman has been asked and has answered the question on several occasions. He indicated that he did not know whether there was an agreement between Boban, Izetbegovic, Tudjman. He stated that very clearly. If you look at his testimony. It's very consistent with his testimony here today. He's saying I don't know if there was an agreement. Now, when you look at the Prosecution's questions it presumes facts that are not in evidence, that have not been agreed upon. Now he can put that question to the witness and the witness can answer it, but he cannot state it as fact. Again, this is sort of the proverbial since when did you stop beating your wife type of question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Not at all. Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you said several times is you don't know whether there were any other agreements or not, and I'm taking what you say at face value, you don't know. So putting aside what you don't know, based on what you did know at the time this was a unilateral order by the HVO that was not legal, being correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, objection. If he doesn't know something then how can he answer that question? If he has all the facts in his command then he can answer the question, but there is a certain element that's missing so how can he presume to say yes this was illegal or not? Assuming that there was no other agreement, yes, it would have of been unilateral.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: But, Mr. Karnavas, I'm a bit lost, because what the Prosecutor just said was literally what he had said in the Kordic case, and the witness has answered yes what you just said is correct. So could he today say it's not correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He indicated that what he said then and what he's saying today is the same. I think we -- at some point you have to stop beating a dead horse. I'm saying he's asked and answered the question. Now, if you wish to put the question to him again we can hear it, but I'm pretty clear that he's answered the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You didn't put it in this way a minute ago. That I could agree. A question put and answered. That I can agree. I can understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I don't have to agree. I only have to understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. You can agree as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you can go next, sir, to Exhibit P 01168, which should be in binder 2. P 01168. This appears to be an order issued by Mr. Halilovic on the 16th of January, 1993, referring to an order that was apparently issued by the -- this order issued or decision, excuse me, decision issued by the HVO HZ HB on January 15th, 1993. Now, directing your attention to the second paragraph in light of the conversation we were having just a moment ago Mr. Halilovic says: "Regarding the fact that the talks in Geneva have not been finished yesterday and that all sides in talks have not signed the documents offered." And that's a true and accurate statement, isn't it? Talks in Geneva had not been finished not and all the sides in the talks had not signed the final documents or any -- or documents, excuse me; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the exact chronology of events before me, but I think that we were already in New York by then. On the 16th of January it's possible that we were already in New York. I cannot say that now but at any rate the Vance-Owen Plan had not been accepted yet in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So this statement is accurate. Regarding the fact that the talks in Geneva have not been finished yet and that all sides in talks have not signed the documents offered is a true and accurate statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but what is referred to is Geneva and the talks were no longer being held in Geneva but in New York.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you can go, please, to Exhibit P 01186. It should be in the same binder, hopefully fairly close to the other one. This appears to be a communication by Arif Pasalic dated the 18th of January, 1993, directed to the HVO Main Staff, responding to an order that's referenced there, the number that we can look at, issued -- informing you in your capacity of chief of the HVO Main Staff in January 1993. That was Mr. Petkovic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that Mr. Petkovic was Chief of Staff of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to look at paragraph number 3. Mr. Pasalic says: "I am informing you that I do recognise the HVO Main Staff as a superior command for coordination of activities on front lines and combat operations against the enemy, Chetniks, and the remnants of the former JNA. "4. Throughout the entire work and all activities I will consider your Command as legally valid as regarding the activities from item 3. "5. I cannot carry out item 2 in your order due to the fact that the 4th Corps of the Bosnian army and its units are not under your command regarding such decisions and there execution." Now, all of those are true and accurate statements, are they not, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I haven't read Mr. Pasalic's letters. This is his letter, and I have nothing to testify about that, but what I can testify to is that after the 15th there was a meeting between Mr. Halilovic and Mr. Petkovic, and they agreed upon something, but I don't know what that was. I did not attend these talks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, it's quite interesting to compare Mr. Pasalic's last document with Halilovic's letter dated January 16. Pasalic is writing on January 18th, two days later. Looks that there are some discrepancies between the two. Halilovic seems to totally reject Mr. Prlic's document, totally reject it. However, when you scrutinise Mr. Pasalic's document or letter, he seems to recognise that there is a superior command, that would be the HVO, this is on item 3, but the difference with Mr. Prlic's document is as to the 4th Corps that would be integrated into the HVO, because he seems to believe or to say that he's not against Mr. Prlic's document. He does recognise that the HVO will be in charge of things, but the 4th Corps would not be dissolved into the HVO. So it looks like things are extremely confused between Halilovic, Pasalic. So if I'm not mistaken, if I understood everything, you didn't know of the ins and outs and you were not aware of all these documents being sent from one to the other, because all of you were in New York at the time. All the politicians and decision-makers were over in New York. So -- so in your back -- in the back of decision-makers, of politician decision-makers, don't you believe that the military were playing their own cards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have already stated to the Honourable Trial Chamber that in the BH army there were certain disagreements. Especially Mr. Halilovic was making decisions on his own. Then this gentleman Mr. Pasalic, he was out of Sarajevo and in a way he was together with the HVO and it seemed to me that he understood the situation better. He was not opposed as you noted and understood so well, Your Honour, whereas Mr. Halilovic was opposed to this. I cannot say with any degree of certainty whether we were in Geneva or New York, and it doesn't matter for these purposes after all, but at any rate we were attending the talks. We would return to Zagreb on the 20th and then went back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But if you, the politicians, had been aware of all these military documents, would you have decided to put a tend to all this and, you know, so that people would understand that there were interferences going on in the negotiation process, or would you have thought that this was quite normal given the circumstances at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We tried, or at least I tried on my part to have the negotiations succeed and for us to abide by the agreements reached. We did abide by quite a few things, but unfortunately many things were done in contravention of the agreements, and many of our agreements or orders were not respected by the military leadership.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, let me put to you, with due respect to the Chamber and to the president, let me put to you a different proposition, and that is in reality, sir, isn't it correct that there is no inconsistency between the Halilovic document and the Pasalic document in this: They both reject implementation of the Prlic decision and a general recognition that in those three provinces, 3, 8, and 10, that the HVO is to either subordinate itself in its entirety -- excuse me, the ABiH is to subordinate itself in its entirety to the HVO or to leave those territories? They both consistently state that position while, while, Mr. Pasalic, perhaps being a bit more nuanced, says well, he agrees that when we're fighting the Serbs we're happy to take our cue from you on an operational basis. But in paragraph 5 of the Pasalic -- Pasalic communication he clearly says, "We are not carrying out the orders as referenced in item 2, to subordinate in general our army to the HVO." Now, that's what the two documents taken together say, don't they?

utterances.speaker: MILE AKMADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but he wouldn't mind having a Joint Command as envisaged. Mr. Prlic's document does not ask for the BH army to be subordinated to the HVO. Rather, both armies should be subordinated in accordance with the peace agreement that was achieved in Geneva. That means that in certain provinces the HVO is in command, and in others the BH army. However, both commands have to include the other structure, too, depending on the number of soldiers and other elements that were discussed in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you've just made exactly the same mistake, I put it to you, that the HVO made in January 1993. You said on page 89, line 24, "The peace agreement that was achieved in Geneva." There was no peace agreement in Geneva in January 1993. It was talks. It was talks, talks, talks. And to use my previous metaphor, the fat lady hadn't sang yet. It was just talks. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Please leave -- let the witness answer and then we will give you the floor. Witness, please answer, and then we will hear the counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said, and I think there is no need for me to repeat this yet again, that the peace plan was finally adopted between the Croats and the Muslims in Washington, the definite one in all segments. In Geneva, all three parties agreed to only what the bare necessities were, and I think that was confirmed by the Security Council, and those are the principles for the BH and the military agreement that I have in my documents that hadn't been signed but that had been agreed upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sir, we'll have to leave your position --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Wait a minute, Mr. Scott. Ms. Tomic wants to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to say that probably this is a language mistake, because my colleague Mr. Scott said to the witness what he said in the first sentence. However, at first and later on, I think this is page 90, line 2 and line 3, he says things that were discussed in Geneva, talked in Geneva, whereas he clearly explained in the continuation of his text what he meant by this. So I think this is a language mistake and that this has to be read fully rather than mislead the witness to the effect that he said something he hadn't meant, but everything becomes obvious when you read the whole answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, on this problem you seem to be contradicting with the Prosecutor. I think I understand what you're saying. In Geneva there were principles that had been accepted by the three parties. There was no plan that had been sign, but at least there was an agreement only the guidelines. Is this what you want to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, correct. I think that the principles were signed too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understand you well, Mr. Prlic's document, according to you, complies with these guidelines and these principles.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prlic's document, the military part of the agreement, is in line with these principles. However, the military negotiations in Geneva, apart from the Plenary Session, took place separately. They were separate from us politicians. The military document was also agreed upon but not sign. What was said was that until there is a complete package, that is to say the borders of the provinces, that is to say the transition government, and everything else that we've talked about here, until all of that is finalised, this is not definitely done, but there was a military agreement that was there by way of an agreement rather than as a definite Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So according to you, there was an agreement on the principles regarding the military aspects, and notably regarding the resubordination of ABiH and HVO units either to one or the other. Is this how we're supposed to understand your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I don't have the plan in front of me right now, but what the plan envisages is first and foremost the end of the conflict. Secondly, withdrawal of units to one's own provinces, one's own, provisionally speaking, nine provinces plus the tenth one is Sarajevo. The withdrawal of Croats and Muslims and certain -- in certain provinces, that can have to do with both segments. And that is where an agreement is reached within the command where both are represented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott, we'll resume tomorrow I'm sure on the same topic, but it's now 7.00 p.m. Witness, let me reassure you, rest assured we're sitting in the morning. Mr. Scott has an hour and 30 minutes left. Mr. Karnavas will have some redirect, but maybe it won't take him two days. We'll see. So with some luck, you might be done tomorrow. That's all I can say so far. I'm not in control of this. I'm not keeping the clock, unfortunately. So Mr. Scott has an hour and 29 minutes left, and we will meet again tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 24th day of June 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.00 p.m.,
